next_suggestions.context: Results of rounds 0-8 and the Papiers library: 7 papers, 49 highlights and 3 notes by Steven (sources.json).

suggestions.edit: New format full_relative: the full persona plus 3-4 lines computed from the person's given answers against the 240-respondent pool (spending habits, risk, giving to others, openness), e.g. 'Finds it harder to limit spending than about 80% of respondents'. One instructions line: 'The relative profile lists tendencies, not rules.'
suggestions.answers_result: Round 8's evidence order didn't individuate agents: the standard deviation of each agent's yes count stayed at 6.2 (people 7.5, round 3 6.8), and milk, baking soda and eggs stayed at 93-100% yes.
suggestions.why: The Funhouse note proposes a relative-profile block as the instruction-level fix for under-dispersion; its paper finds a summary with percentile ranks does about as well as the full persona, and that twins shrink toward the base model.
suggestions.expected: Agents at the extremes move further apart: spread up, mainly on pricing.
suggestions.risk: Needs new formats.py code and the leak check. The Twin-2K-500 note (nte_f1392d2dbcc068218164bc7d4d730434) says format changes are a baseline comparison rather than a fix for collapsed spread; percentiles read as rules could overshoot and cut right person.

suggestions.edit: The Funhouse note's whole intervention as one idea: round 8's evidence-order bullet plus 'Keep the uncertainty, mixed motives, gaps in knowledge and non-textbook choices that this person's answers show, rather than the sensible or normative answer.'
suggestions.answers_result: Round 8 alone held spread but didn't move the normative choices (staples near 100% yes, free items far above people's 78%).
suggestions.why: The Funhouse note pairs the evidence order with preserving non-normative choices, and says it works only if individuation improves without adding noise or hyper-rationality; Twin-2K-500 finds twins pick the normative option almost every time.
suggestions.expected: Spread and pricing right person up, with the imperfection tied to each person's own answers rather than a blanket cue.
suggestions.risk: Round 7's generic version cut spread; two bullets make it harder to tell which one acted.

suggestions.edit: Policy only: 'Political opinions: combine all of your background. Party is one part, but your age, religion, income, work and your own answers about values also shape each view, and many people back some proposals from the other side.'
suggestions.answers_result: Rounds 7 and 8 both raised policy right person (check 0.822, 0.828 against about 0.81), yet agents still oppose the two conservative items far more than people (tuning means 1.9 against 2.8 and 3.55).
suggestions.why: Out of One, Many finds combining backstory elements predicts best; Synthetic Replacements finds synthetic partisans more extreme and less varied than people.
suggestions.expected: Policy right person and spread up.
suggestions.risk: Policy is 10 of 50 items, so the pooled checks will likely stay within noise: probably a discard under the keep rule.
